newsitem.title: CHINA: China woos Taiwan with 'one country, two systems'.
newsitem.headline: China woos Taiwan with 'one country, two systems'.

text.p: Premier Li Peng on Tuesday hailed the resumption of Chinese sovereignty over Hong Kong as a new era and wooed rival Taiwan by suggesting reunification under a similar recovery formula.

"This is not only to celebrate the start of a new era for Hong Kong, it is also to celebrate a major victory in the peaceful reunification of China," Li told about 4,000 people at a reception in Beijing to celebrate China's recovery of sovereignty over Hong Kong at midnight on Monday.
Reunification was a major theme of his speech hours after the end of what China saw as 156 years of humiliating colonial rule by Britain over Hong Kong.
"The 'one country, two systems' formula works for Hong Kong and Macau," Li said. "It can also work for Taiwan."

Under the "one country, two systems" formula devised by the late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, Beijing has promised to allow Hong Kong to keep its capitalist lifestyle for 50 years after the transfer to Chinese sovereignty.

It was the first time since Beijing recovered its new special region that China had so explicitly suggested to Taiwan, which it regards as a renegade province, that it should follow Hong Kong's example.
Taiwan's Nationalists, who lost the Chinese civil war to the Communists and fled into exile on the island in 1949, have rejected the formula, insisting on reunification under a democratic system.
"The Republic of China government (on Taiwan) will never accept such a formula," government spokesman David Lee said on Tuesday in response to Premier Li's remarks.
Li was adamant Taiwan would return to the fold.

"No matter how many difficulties we meet on the road ahead, we must certainly realise complete reunification of the motherland," Li told the reception at the Great Hall of the People. "It can also certainly be realised."
The next outpost of a colonial empire to return to China will be Macau, a Portuguese-run enclave about 40 km (25 miles) west of Hong Kong that reverts to Beijing in 1999.
Li shrugged off worries about Hong Kong's future, saying Hong Kong affairs were now China's internal affair.
Western governments and international human rights groups have criticised moves to curb civil liberties in post-colonial Hong Kong.

While Hong Kong's own confidence in China's "one country, two systems" pledge was dented in June 1989 when Chinese soldiers backed by tanks crushed student-led demonstrations for democracy in Beijing's Tiananmen Square, killing hundreds.
Li moved to allay any fears, saying the central government would not interfere in anything that should, under Hong Kong's mini-constitution, be decided by Hong Kong people themselves.
"We believe that long-term prosperity and stability will surely be maintained in Hong Kong as long as the basic guidelines and policies are earnestly implemented," Li said.
Li said a democratic system that was consistent with Hong Kong's basic law and suited the territory's circumstances would develop gradually.
"Hong Kong compatriots will surely enjoy extensive rights and freedom unparalleled during the colonial rule," he said.

Hong Kong's democrats fear the freedom of the press and multi-party politics may vanish in the territory after a Beijing-anointed legislature replaced the enclave's democratically elected lawmaking body early on the first day of Beijing rule.
